Where it began

Gary Kirsten was born in Cape Town on 23 November 1967 and went to Rondebosch Boys' High School. He played his domestic cricket close to home, for Western Province, from 1987 until 2004.

His Test career began against Australia in Melbourne in 1993. From there he made the top of South Africa's order his own for more than a decade.

The player

Kirsten played 101 Tests between 1993 and 2004. A left-hander who mostly opened, he scored 7,289 runs at 45.27, with 21 hundreds and 34 fifties, and held 84 catches. He was the first South African to reach 100 Tests, a milestone that came against New Zealand. He also led his country once, in a drawn Test.

His best-known innings was 275 against England at Kingsmead in Durban. South Africa had been made to follow on, and he batted for more than fourteen hours to save them. It ranks among the longest innings, by time, that Test cricket has seen. He was also the first batsman to make Test hundreds against all nine other Test nations.

What made him special

He was patient above all. Kirsten would wait, and wait, for a bad ball. When a game needed quicker runs, he could find another gear. In one-day cricket he made 188 not out against the United Arab Emirates at the 1996 World Cup, and he was part of the side that won the 1998 ICC KnockOut Trophy. He signed off from Tests in 2004 with 76 in his final innings to help beat New Zealand. Wisden made him one of its Cricketers of the Year.

Away from the middle

Coaching made him just as well known. He took charge of India in 2008, and in his time India won Test and one-day series in New Zealand for the first time in 40 years. His time ended with the 2011 World Cup final at the Wankhede Stadium, where India beat Sri Lanka. Suresh Raina, Yusuf Pathan and Virat Kohli lifted him onto their shoulders for a lap of the ground.

Back with South Africa from 2011 to 2013, he saw his home side reach number one in the Test rankings in August 2012. Later came spells with the Hobart Hurricanes, Royal Challengers Bangalore and Gujarat Titans, and in April 2026 he began as head coach of Sri Lanka.

And finally

He took two Test wickets in his career, and one of them cost him nothing at all: his best figures were 1 for 0. Most part-time bowlers would happily settle for that.
